analysis.one_liner: Makes clothing brands legally responsible for sweatshop wage and child-labor violations by their contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it died in the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997, having no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed the Fair Labor Standards Act so that clothing manufacturers and retailers who hire outside sewing shops are legally liable, alongside those contractors, for violating minimum wage, overtime, child labor, and industrial homework rules. It would also have set fines of up to $1,000 per worker for failing to keep payroll records, and fines of $10,000 or more for submitting fake payroll records that hide hours worked or wage violations. The goal was to stop brands from shifting production to contractors who pay below minimum wage, and to make it easier for the Labor Department to collect back wages for workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Garment workers, many of them low-wage and immigrant, who are shorted on wages or forced to work improper hours in contractor shops: the bill would have let them recover from the brand or retailer that profited from the work, not just from a small contractor that may vanish. Law-abiding garment makers would also have gained a level playing field, since the bill's findings note that sweatshops compete unfairly against employers who follow the law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage garment workers and compliant employers

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers and retailers who contract out garment work would be jointly and severally liable, to the same extent as the contractor, for violations of minimum wage, overtime, child labor, and industrial homework rules in producing their apparel [S3].
Workers shorted on wages could recover from the manufacturer in the garment industry, not only from the contractor who employed them [S3].

Employers who fail to keep required payroll records would face a civil penalty of up to $1,000 per affected employee, and anyone submitting fraudulent payroll records to conceal actual hours or wage violations would face penalties of $10,000 per act, or $15,000 for a repeat offense [S3].

The bill's findings cite the Comptroller General's conclusion that most sweatshop employers violate the law's recordkeeping requirements, which hampers the Labor Department's ability to collect wages owed to workers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Apparel manufacturers and retailers who use outside contractors would bear the cost of monitoring their supply chains and paying penalties and back wages when contractors break the law. Sweatshop contractors would face steeper and more certain penalties. Some of this cost could pass through to clothing prices.

drawbacks.text: Holding brands jointly liable for contractor violations could push apparel companies to move production overseas, where the law does not reach, which would cost domestic garment jobs — the very workers the bill aims to protect [S3].
Compliance and monitoring costs for manufacturers and retailers would likely be passed on to consumers in the form of higher clothing prices [S3].
The new recordkeeping fines add enforcement burdens and paperwork costs for small apparel businesses, on top of the Fair Labor Standards Act's existing requirements [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real, documented problem: contractors that underpay or overwork garment workers while the brands profiting from the work escaped liability, and missing or fake payroll records blocked recovery of back wages. The main honest costs are that brands might relocate production abroad and that some compliance costs could reach consumers. Whether those costs outweigh the wage recovery and deterrence depends on how aggressively the Labor Department enforced the new liability; the bill contained no special funding for enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 1996 and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never acted on it before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on September 25, 1996, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5].
No committee or floor action followed; the bill had no cosponsors [S4] [S5].
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and bills not acted on expire with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Apparel manufacturers, retailers, and contractors who rely on low-wage subcontracting are better off, because they never faced joint liability for wage, hour, and child labor violations in their supply chains. Workers owed back wages in sweatshop conditions gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Sweatshops Act of 1996 and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled any action on it during the remainder of the 104th Congress.

against.name: Nancy Kassebaum
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, did not bring the bill to a markup or vote in the months it sat before the committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and no roll-call votes were ever taken, so the fight never took a measurable partisan shape — though no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill would have made them jointly liable for wage, hour, and child labor violations committed by the contractors producing their clothing, along with new penalties tied to their own contractors' violations. Killing the bill preserved their ability to profit from subcontracted production without legal responsibility for conditions in the shops.

With the bill dead, contractors that violate minimum wage, overtime, and child labor rules face only the existing enforcement tools, and the bill's findings note that poor recordkeeping already hampers recovery of back wages. Brands would have had a direct financial stake in policing them under the bill; without it, that pressure is absent.
The bill's own findings say sweatshops give an unfair competitive edge over employers who obey the law, so the bill's failure leaves compliant employers still competing against violators.
